art.text: Over the 16th century, the central and eastern Maghreb, meaning Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, came under Ottoman control. Architecture in Morocco stayed largely traditional. In Algeria and Tunisia it blended with Ottoman architecture, especially in the coastal cities where Ottoman influence was strongest.

In the late 16th century the Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur built the Badi Palace in Marrakesh, a lavish reception palace. It was essentially a giant rectangular riad courtyard, with symmetrical gardens, pools, and two monumental pavilions facing each other at either end.
The Sidi Mahrez Mosque was the first and only Ottoman-style domed mosque in Tunisia. It was begun by Muhammad Bey and completed by his successor, Ramadan ibn Murad, between 1696 and 1699.

The largest riad garden in Marrakesh today is the Arsat an-Nil, or Garden of the Nile, in the Royal Palace. It dates from the reign of the Alaouite sultan Muhammad Ibn Abdallah (1757 to 1790). It measures around 130 meters north to south and 70 meters east to west.

The prayer hall of the Sidi Mahrez Mosque is covered by a dome system typical of Classical Ottoman architecture. It has a large central dome flanked by four semi-domes, with four smaller domes at the corners. Sinan first used this arrangement for the Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul, around 1548.

Some European influences were introduced into the architecture of Algeria and Tunisia during Ottoman times, particularly through the importation of materials from Italy such as marble. In the same period, port cities such as Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli became centers of pirate activity, which brought wealth to local elites but also attracted intrusions by European powers, who occupied and fortified some coastal positions.

The two monumental pavilions facing each other in the Badi Palace's courtyard recalled the layout of a much smaller space, the Court of the Lions in the Alhambra. The Badi Palace was built by the Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur in Marrakesh.
Ahmad al-Mansur also built a Saadian palace in the Agdal Gardens, which had a symmetrical riad-style courtyard layout. Modern structures have since replaced it.
Inside the Sidi Mahrez Mosque, the walls are decorated with marble paneling and Ottoman Iznik tiles. The decoration matches the mosque's Ottoman dome system, which was built between 1696 and 1699.

war.text: The Maghrebi war of 1699 to 1702 pitted a Tunisian, Tripolitanian and Moroccan coalition against the Regency of Algiers. Both sides ignored the Ottoman sultan's pleas to sign a peace treaty. The war marked a further weakening of the already fragile Ottoman grip over the Maghreb.

Alaouite sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif repeatedly tried to take over the Beylik of Mascara, and every attempt ended in defeat. The failures came in 1672 at Tlemcen, 1678 at the Oued Za, 1692 at the Moulouya, 1693 in Oran and 1694 in Djidiouïa.

Ismail led a large army of up to 50,000 men against the Dey of Algiers. Although the Algerians were outnumbered, they won a great victory and killed about 3,000 Moroccans. The defeat led to a ceasefire between Algiers and Morocco, which let the Dey focus on Tunis instead.
The Battle of Moulouya in 1692 ended in an Algerian victory. The Algerians pushed the Moroccans back all the way to Fez.

In 1699 to 1700 a Moroccan army, mainly composed of the Black Guard, entered Algeria under Ismail's son Zidan. The Bey of Mascara, Mustapha Bouchelaghem, was unprepared, so the invasion was swift. At Tlemcen the Moroccans besieged a city defended by armed Kouloughlis, its main inhabitants.

The Algerian hold on Tunis did not last. In 1695 the Tunisians revolted and defeated ben Cheker at the battle of Kairouan, reinstating the Muradid dynasty. This ended the short-lived Algerian Beylik of Tunis.

After Tlemcen fell, the Moroccan army advanced to Mascara and looted the Bey's palace. Despite this success, the campaign ended in a peace negotiation that infuriated Moulay Ismail. He then directed another offensive against the Algerians.

On 3 October 1700 Algerian forces defeated the armies of Murad at the Battle of Jouami' al' Ulama near Sétif. The defeat caused a rout, and Murad had to retreat into Tunisian territory, abandoning all of his gains.
The Maghrebi war renewed the infighting among the Muradids. That infighting would later lead to the establishment of the Beylik of Tunis and the Husainid dynasty in 1705.

Zidan's achievements in Algeria are apparently unknown to contemporary comment and may be assumed to be fiction. In September of the same year, a Moroccan prince on a minor tax raid in Tlemcen was defeated by an Algerian battalion.
Even after his defeat, Murad tried to raise another army in hopes of attacking Algeria again. He sent his commander Ibrahim Sharif to Constantinople to recruit additional janissaries.

literature.text: The Moroccan Sufi scholar Al-Hasan al-Yusi, considered the greatest Moroccan scholar of the seventeenth century, wrote an autobiography called Al-Fahrasa. Only its introduction and first section survive, and until recently they were unpublished. They frankly discuss his childhood misdeeds and the pleasures of his conjugal sex life, among other intimate details.

Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of the Saadi dynasty, who ruled Morocco from 1578 to 1603, was described as a lover of books and calligraphy and a connoisseur of mystical texts. He also enjoyed scholarly discussions at his court.

The scholar Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti was deported to Fez, Morocco, in 1594 after the Moroccan invasion of Songhai, staying there until Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's death and only reaching Timbuktu again on April 22, 1608. While in Morocco he wrote much of the work for which he became noted, including a biography of the jurist Muhammad Abd al-Karim al-Maghili.

Al-Yusi's better known text, called Al-Muhadrat or Discourses, also contains many autobiographical passages. Like Al-Fahrasa, it is remarkable for its frank discussion of childhood misdeeds, the pleasures of his conjugal sex life, and other intimate details of his personal life.
Al-Yusi also wrote a Daliyya, a poem of praise, honoring his Sufi teacher Muhammad b. Nasir al-Dari of the Zawiya Nasiriyya in Tamegroute. The poem became famous both in Morocco and in West Africa.

Al-Ayyashi traveled to the Hejaz three times, in 1649, 1653 and 1661, staying for long periods in Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem and Cairo. He wrote a two-volume rihla about these journeys called Ma' al-Mawa'id.

Before becoming sultan, Ahmad al-Mansur spent 17 years among the Ottomans and received an extensive education that included poetry, grammar, lexicography and exegesis alongside other Islamic and secular sciences. This literary grounding shaped the cultured court he later kept in Morocco.

Abd al-Qadir al-Fasi's biography, titled Tuhfat al-Kebir, was written by his son, Abd al-Rahman al-Fasi. It offers insight into the life of the Sufi scholar who founded the Shadhili zawiyya of Ksar-el-Kebir.

In his works Al-Fahrasa and Al-Muhadrat, the Moroccan scholar Al-Hasan al-Yusi frankly discussed his own childhood misdeeds and the pleasures of his conjugal sex life, along with other intimate details of his personal life. The article calls both texts remarkable for this frankness.
Al-Hasan al-Yusi wrote a poem of praise, the Daliyya, honoring his teacher Muhammad b. Nasir al-Dari of the Zawiya Nasiriyya in Tamegroute. The poem became famous across Morocco and West Africa.

science.text: Ahmad al-Mansur, Saadi Sultan of Morocco from 1578 to 1603, received an extensive education in secular sciences including geometry, arithmetic, algebra, and astronomy, alongside Islamic law and theology. He was known as a lover of books, calligraphy and mathematics, and enjoyed scholarly discussions.

Leo Africanus, born al-Hasan al-Wazzan al-Fasi, completed a manuscript on the geography of Africa in 1526 while living in Rome. Published in Italian in 1550 as Description of Africa, it was regarded among European scholars as the most authoritative treatise on the region until the modern exploration of Africa.

After leaving Rome following the death of his patron Pope Leo X in 1521, Leo Africanus stayed in Bologna, where he wrote an Arabic-Hebrew-Latin medical vocabulary and a grammar of Arabic. Only the Arabic part of the vocabulary and an eight-page fragment of the grammar have survived to today.
Al-Mansur employed French physicians at his court in Morocco. Arnoult de Lisle served him from 1588 to 1598, and was then succeeded by Étienne Hubert d'Orléans, who served from 1598 to 1600.

Both of Ahmad al-Mansur's French court physicians later returned to France and became professors of Arabic at the Collège de France. Arnoult de Lisle and Étienne Hubert d'Orléans also continued diplomatic work between Morocco and France after leaving the sultan's service.

politics.text: Sultan al-Rashid, who ruled from 1666 to 1672, was the first Alawi ruler to establish his authority over the entire country of Morocco. His successor Moulay Isma'il, who reigned from 1672 to 1727, took the sultanate to its peak of political power with strong central rule that was also brutal. He enforced heavy taxation, led an army of Black slaves loyal to him alone, and had Christian captives forced into labour on his construction projects until they were ransomed. European writers gave him a reputation for ruthlessness and cruelty.

After the fall of Granada in 1492, Arabs and Muslims in Al-Andalus faced persecution under Christian Spanish rule. In 1609 Spain carried out the Expulsion of the Moriscos, which aimed to forcibly remove all Muslims from the Iberian Peninsula. About 275,000 to 300,000 people were expelled, and many settled in Maghreb cities such as Fez, Tlemcen and Tunis.

Corsairs became agents of the Ottoman Empire and made Algiers their base, among them the brothers Khair al-Din and Aruj, both called Barbarossa for their red beards. Another, Uluj Ali, seized Tunis in 1569. After a Spanish recapture in 1573, he returned in 1574 with a large fleet and army to take it for good.

Moroccan authors of the Alawi period classified their state as both a caliphate and an imamate. It was an absolute monarchy with no clear rules of succession, which helps explain the turmoil after some rulers died.

Jews had already faced periods of persecution in the Maghreb, and in the 14th to 16th centuries many fled Spain and Portugal because of growing persecution and the Spanish Inquisition. After Spain expelled its Jews in 1492 and Portugal forced mass conversions in 1497, many Sephardic Jews settled in North Africa. They founded new communities and merged with the existing Jewish populations of the Maghreb.
The Alawi dynasty came to power in the 17th century with help from Arab tribes. It mobilized them against the powerful Berber principality of Dila'iyyah.

The Corsican Murad Curso, who died in 1631, followed his sponsor Ramdan Bey into the office of Bey and was later also named Pasha. His son Hamuda inherited both titles with the backing of Tunis notables. In 1640 Hamuda Bey moved to control appointments to the office of Dey.

Husayn ibn Ali, a cavalry officer of Greek Cretan origin, came to power in Tunis in 1705. He won support from the ulama, notables and tribes by opposing Algerian influence, which was removed. Yet his nephew Ali and his son Muhammad later fought a civil war over the succession.

After Moulay Isma'il's death, northern Morocco became virtually independent under Ahmad ar-Rifi, who ruled from Tangier. He profited from an arms trade with the British at Gibraltar and established diplomatic relations with them. He invaded Fez in 1741 and was defeated and killed in 1743.

In 1747, Sultan Abdallah made his two sons viceroys, or Khalifa, in politically important cities. Mawlay Ahmed governed Rabat and Sidi Mohammed governed Marrakesh. The eldest died in 1750, and Abdallah himself died in 1757.

philosophy.text: Ahmad al-Tijani was born in Algeria and became a Sufi teacher. In 1781 he experienced a vision of Muhammad that he believed commanded him to found his own order, the Tijaniyyah.
Ahmad al-Tijani founded the Tijaniyya Sufi order in Boussemghoun, Algeria, sometime between 1781 and 1784. New members had to receive the Tijani wird, a sequence of holy phrases repeated twice daily.
Al-Hasan al-Yusi, who lived from 1631 to 1691, is considered the greatest Moroccan scholar of the seventeenth century. He was also a close associate of Rashid, the first Alaouite sultan of Morocco.

Morocco's Alawi sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif, who ruled from 1672 to 1727, created a pilgrimage to the tombs of the Seven Saints of Marrakesh. The move was partly meant to counter the popularity of a rival Berber saints' pilgrimage near Essaouira.

Before founding his own Sufi order, Ahmad al-Tijani studied Islamic jurisprudence through Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Jundi's Maliki-rite writings. He also read Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri's Sufi treatise, the Risala ila al-sufiyya.
In 1757 Ahmad al-Tijani left his village for Fez, Morocco. There he joined three Sufi brotherhoods at once: the Qadiriyya, the Nasiriyya, and the tariqa of Ahmad al-Habib b. Muhammed.

To organize the new Seven Saints pilgrimage in Marrakesh, sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif entrusted the task to the scholar Al-Hasan al-Yusi. Al-Yusi was chosen for his familiarity with the country's zawiyas, or Sufi brotherhood institutions.
During his travels, Ahmad al-Tijani received Mahmud al-Kurdi's blessing in Cairo to preach the Khalwatiyya order. He then settled for a couple of years at Tlemcen.

Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah was known for leaning toward Wahhabism, a puritanical school of thought opposed to venerating saints. Even so, he patronized and expanded the zawiyas and shrines of the Seven Saints of Marrakesh.

culture.text: The Char Bouba war was fought in modern-day Western Sahara and Mauritania from 1644 to 1674. During it, Hassani Arab communities enriched themselves by collecting tolls from trade caravans and extorting farming and herding villages in the oases. After decades of confrontations the native Berber population was completely Arabized, and its language and culture were destroyed. The war gave rise to the contemporary Sahrawi people.

Christian institutions lingered in Marrakesh well into the Early Modern era. The city's bishopric continued to exist until the late 16th century, and Franciscan monasteries remained there until the 18th century.

The Moriscos were refugees who had been forcibly expelled from the Iberian Peninsula after persecution under Christian Spanish rule. Being accustomed to urban life, they settled in cities. In Morocco they chose Fez, Rabat and Tangier, in Algeria Tlemcen and Constantine, and in Tunisia Kairouan, Tunis and Bizerte.

The Moriscos brought the urban dialects of Andalusi Arabic with them and introduced these to the existing Bedouin Arabic dialects of the Maghreb. This event greatly increased the process of Arabization in the region from the 15th to the 17th century.

During the Char Bouba war, which ran from 1644 to 1674 in modern-day Western Sahara and Mauritania, Hassani communities enriched themselves by collecting tolls from trade caravans. They also extorted farming and herding villages settled in the oases. After decades of confrontations, the war ended up completely Arabizing the native Berber population, destroying their language and culture and giving rise to the contemporary Sahrawi people.
Juan de Prado had attempted to re-establish the Christian mission in Marrakesh, but he was killed in 1631.
